summary:
Oyo State stands under the Nigerian national framework, and that framework applies in full to visitors. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Act also reaches assisting, attending or promoting same-sex ceremonies, so guests at a private union are exposed as well as the couple.

Sexual conduct itself is separately criminal. Oyo is a southern state governed by the Criminal Code, which penalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. Oyo lies outside the Shari'a regime, so the death penalty for male same-sex conduct that operates under state Zina provisions does not apply here; twelve northern states do apply it, and visitors crossing into them carry that exposure.

Gender expression is a live risk even though trans identity is not named in the statute. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians live under threat of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available.

Enforcement in Oyo takes the form of police profiling, entrapment and extortion of people perceived as gay, an extortion practice commonly called kito. A young man stopped by Lagos police in March 2025 was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay. Mass arrests recur nationally: 42 men in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a Delta hotel raid in June 2018, 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023.

Dating apps are a documented vector. BBC Africa Eye reported on 15 May 2023 that criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular apps, entrap men, film them, then extort, beat and kidnap them; the investigation interviewed 21 people who had been kito'd, and victims do not report to police for fear of arrest or attack. The Thomson Reuters Foundation documented the same pattern in April 2024, with victims blackmailed with threats of outing. Gay and transgender app users in Oyo face this risk as elsewhere in Nigeria.

Trans people face killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the federal capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months later no suspects had been charged.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
The dating-app entrapment economy described by BBC Africa Eye is Lagos-based in its reporting, but the underlying practice is described as applying across Nigeria, and Oyo shares a border and a metropolitan continuum with Lagos State.

Police conduct independent of the statute produces much of the practical risk. Those affected describe the 2014 Act as a weaponised law that generates a climate of hostility even where no charge is brought, and extortion demands are meted out on the basis of appearance rather than evidence.

Partial enforcement is also documented. The same BBC Africa Eye investigation showed a police commander vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of officers catching a kito suspect, so the apparatus aimed at gangs and at victims is not identical.

Corrections practice has drawn official censure. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations against the authorities but found that housing Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
localsOnly:
Residents of Oyo State live under the Criminal Code as well as the 2014 Act, with sex between men carrying up to 14 years and gross indecency up to 3 years; the registering, operating or participating in LGBT organisations is separately punishable with up to 14 years.

No anti-discrimination protection exists at national or state level, so employment, housing and service refusal on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity carry no legal remedy.

Bobrisky pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, serving the term in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion.

Community reporting to police is discouraged by outcome: people who are kito'd tend not to report, fearing arrest or further attack, and the mass-arrest series shows that gatherings and premises can be raided wholesale.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted is unresolved; the sources available record only the proposals and the fear they generated.

No Oyo-specific incident series, state enforcement divergence or regional protective statute appears in this inventory. The absence of a recorded Oyo case is an absence of sourcing, not a finding that none exists.

Whether the Correctional Service Act finding on Bobrisky's placement produced any change to placement policy for transgender detainees is not sourced here.

The FCDO advisory is reported through a secondary account of the 2026 travel advice; the advisory text itself has not been consulted directly.
